name: Iceland
traditionNote: A Nordic system built on statute rather than on codes, where the courts review legislation against the constitution in ordinary cases and the Supreme Court's reasoning is followed as a matter of practice rather than of doctrine.
summary: Acts (lög) are passed by the Alþingi, a single chamber of 63 members, and confirmed by the President, who may instead refuse and send the act to a referendum — a power used three times, all since 2004. An act is published in the A division of Stjórnartíðindi, and publication is what makes it binding: the Act on Stjórnartíðindi and Lögbirtingablað no. 15/2005 governs the whole system and provides that no one may be required to obey a rule before it has been published. Regulations (reglugerðir) made by ministers under a statutory authorisation go into the B division, along with the by-laws and planning notices of municipalities, and treaties into the C division. There is no constitutional court: the ordinary courts, since 2018 in three tiers, decide constitutional questions in the cases before them. Iceland is not in the EU but is in the European Economic Area, so a large body of EU legislation applies after being taken into the EEA Agreement and implemented by Icelandic act or regulation, with the EFTA Court and the EFTA Surveillance Authority standing where the EU institutions would.
hierarchy: Stjórnarskrá lýðveldisins Íslands nr. 33/1944 (Constitution), including the human rights chapter rewritten in 1995
Lög — acts of the Alþingi, among them the act incorporating the European Convention on Human Rights
EEA rules as implemented by Icelandic act or regulation, with the EEA Act directing that implemented EEA provisions prevail over other statutory rules
Reglugerðir — ministerial regulations made under an authorisation in an act
Gjaldskrár and auglýsingar — tariffs and official notices with legal effect, published in the B division
Samþykktir sveitarfélaga — municipal by-laws, confirmed by the responsible ministry and published in the B division
Administrative practice and guidance, which binds the administration and not the citizen

gazette.name: Stjornartidindi
gazette.authority: Dómsmálaráðuneytið (Ministry of Justice); published on Ísland.is under Act no. 15/2005
gazette.coverage: Division A for acts and the instruments equated with them, B for regulations, tariffs, by-laws and notices, C for treaties; electronic publication under the 2005 Act, with the earlier printed series digitised
gazette.desc: The gazette that makes an Icelandic rule binding. Its three divisions sort the corpus by rank before you read a word: an act is in A, a ministerial regulation or a municipal planning notice in B, a treaty in C. The B division is the busiest by a wide margin, which is itself a fact about where Icelandic law is made.
gazette.howto: The front page lists the newest notices with their division, publication date and number — 895/2026 B deild is number 895 of 2026 in the B division, and that number plus year is the citation. The shortcuts split the collection into Lög, Reglugerðir, Gjaldskrár and Auglýsendur, and the subject categories narrow it further.
gazette.note: Act no. 15/2005 also governs Lögbirtingablað, the separate notice gazette for summonses, bankruptcies and compulsory sales; its own site is often unreachable from outside Iceland.

constitution.name: Stjornarskra lydveldisins Islands
constitution.en: Constitution of the Republic of Iceland
constitution.authority: Adopted by referendum and enacted on the founding of the republic, 17 June 1944; maintained in the Lagasafn by the Alþingi
constitution.coverage: In force since 17 June 1944, amended several times, most substantially in 1995 when the human rights chapter was rewritten
constitution.desc: A short constitution inherited in outline from the Danish one of 1849 and never replaced, despite the elaborate post-crash attempt of 2010 to 2013 — a constituent assembly, a draft and a consultative referendum that approved it, none of which the Alþingi enacted. Judicial review of legislation is not written into it and is nonetheless settled practice.
constitution.howto: Read the consolidated text in the Alþingi's Lagasafn; the Prime Minister's Office publishes an English translation at government.is. Amendment requires the Alþingi to pass the change, dissolve, and the newly elected Alþingi to pass it again unaltered.
constitution.note: The Alþingi site sits behind a Cloudflare challenge and answers automated requests with a holding page; it serves browsers normally.

sources.name: Lagasafn
sources.en: The consolidated collection of Icelandic acts
sources.coverage: Acts in force, consolidated and reissued after each parliamentary session, with the edition dated on its front page
sources.desc: The working text of Icelandic statute law, maintained by the parliament itself. It is a periodic edition rather than a continuously updated one: the collection states the session it is current to, and anything passed since must be picked up from the gazette.
sources.howto: Browse by subject or by act number and year — the Constitution is 1944 number 33, which resolves as /lagas/nuna/1944033.html — or search the text. Each act shows the amending acts against the provisions they changed.
sources.note: Consolidated to the stated session only, and behind a Cloudflare challenge for automated requests. The published text in Stjórnartíðindi is the authentic one.

sources.name: Althingi
sources.coverage: Bills (frumvörp) with their explanatory memoranda, committee opinions, readings and votes, by session; parliamentary questions and reports; the record of debates
sources.desc: The parliament that has met, in one form or another, since 930. For legal work its value is the greinargerð — the explanatory memorandum published with every bill — which Icelandic courts use in the same way Nordic courts generally use preparatory works.
sources.howto: Find a bill by session and number (þingskjal), read the greinargerð, and follow the committee opinions and readings to the version passed. The site is bilingual in outline, with the legislative material itself in Icelandic.
sources.note: Behind a Cloudflare challenge for automated requests; browsers are served normally.

sources.name: Reglugerdasafn
sources.authority: Dómsmálaráðuneytið and the ministries, published on Ísland.is
sources.coverage: Ministerial regulations in force, consolidated where amendments have been merged, arranged by number and by ministry
sources.desc: Where most operative Icelandic law actually is. An act delegates and a reglugerð fills in, so the rule that decides a matter is more often here than in the Lagasafn — the collection is comparatively new and carries its own reservations about completeness.
sources.howto: Browse the newest regulations or search by number, title and issuing ministry; the advanced search narrows by field. Each regulation cites the act it is made under, which is the test of whether it is validly made.
sources.note: The collection states that it is a first edition and asks users to read its reservations; the published item in Stjórnartíðindi B remains the authentic text.

sources.name: Haestirettur Islands
sources.coverage: The Court's judgments and its decisions on applications for leave to appeal, the hearing schedule, cases under appeal, and English summaries of selected cases
sources.desc: The final instance since 1920, and since the 2018 reform the third tier rather than the second: appeals now run district court, Landsréttur, and then to the Supreme Court only with leave, granted where the case has precedential value or is otherwise significant.
sources.howto: Use 'Dómaleit' to search judgments across the courts and 'Dagskrá' for the schedule; the decisions granting or refusing leave are published separately under 'Ákvarðanir um áfrýjunar- og kæruleyfi'. 'Legal Summaries of Selected Cases' is the English window.
sources.note: Because leave is required, the Supreme Court now decides a small number of cases a year; much of what would once have been its work ends at Landsréttur.

sources.name: Landsrettur
sources.coverage: Judgments and rulings of the appeal court since it began sitting on 1 January 2018, with its hearing schedule
sources.desc: The middle tier created in 2018 to give Iceland a full appellate court between the district courts and the Supreme Court — and the subject of the Strasbourg judgment in Guðmundur Andri Ástráðsson, which held that irregularities in appointing its judges breached the right to a tribunal established by law.
sources.howto: Search the judgments by case number or date; case numbers run by year. Its decisions are final unless the Supreme Court grants leave to appeal.
sources.note: Because most cases now end here, Landsréttur judgments carry much of the practical weight that Supreme Court judgments used to.

sources.name: Domstolar
sources.coverage: The eight district courts, the appeal court, the Supreme Court and the Court of Reopening, with their judgments, rules and hearing lists
sources.desc: The entry point to the whole judiciary, including the district courts whose judgments are published — unusually, since most systems publish only appellate decisions — and the Endurupptökudómur, a separate court created to decide applications to reopen concluded cases.
sources.howto: Use the shared case search across courts, or go to an individual district court for its own lists; the judicial administration publishes the procedural rules and the fees.
sources.note: Judgments are published with names in many cases, in contrast with the anonymisation practised elsewhere in the Nordic countries.

sources.name: Samradsgatt
sources.coverage: Draft bills, draft regulations and policy documents put out for comment, with the responses received and the ministry's summary of them
sources.desc: The stage before a bill exists. Ministries publish drafts here for public comment, which is the earliest point at which a rule is visible — and often the only point at which a regulation, which never goes to parliament, is visible before it is published in the gazette.
sources.howto: Browse open and closed consultations by ministry and status; each case shows the draft, the deadline, every comment submitted and, when the consultation closes, what the ministry did with them.
sources.note: A draft here is not law and often changes substantially before it is.

sources.name: Umbodsmadur Althingis
sources.authority: Umboðsmaður Alþingis, elected by the Alþingi
sources.coverage: Opinions on complaints and own-initiative cases, annual reports, and the monitoring of places of detention
sources.desc: The main published authority on Icelandic administrative law: how a ministry must reason a decision, when a licence may be refused, what counts as an adequate investigation of a case. Its opinions are followed by the administration and cited in court.
sources.howto: Search the opinions by year and case number or by subject; each states the authority, the provisions and the conclusion, and the follow-up where the authority responded.
sources.note: An opinion binds nobody, but the practice of administrative law in Iceland is largely built out of them.

sources.name: EFTA Surveillance Authority
sources.coverage: Decisions, reasoned opinions and infringement cases concerning Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway under the EEA Agreement, and the state aid register
sources.desc: Iceland is in the internal market through the EEA Agreement rather than through EU membership, and this authority — with the EFTA Court beside it — performs for the EEA states what the Commission and the Court of Justice do for EU members. Its decisions are where EEA obligations are enforced against Iceland.
sources.howto: Search the decisions and cases by state and subject; state aid decisions have their own register. For the EEA rules themselves, work from the annexes of the EEA Agreement to the Icelandic act or regulation that implements them.
sources.note: EU regulations do not apply in Iceland of their own force. There is always an Icelandic implementing instrument, and it is that instrument which binds.

sources.name: Government of Iceland (English)
sources.coverage: English translations of the Constitution and of selected acts and regulations, published by the ministries
sources.desc: What exists of Icelandic law in English. Coverage is thin and driven by whichever fields need to be readable abroad — fisheries, foreign investment, financial regulation, data protection — and the Constitution.
sources.howto: Browse the legislation section of the publications list; the Constitution is on the constitution topic page with its own PDF. Check the date on any translation, since several are frozen at the version current when they were made.
sources.note: Translations are unofficial and have no legal force; only the Icelandic text does.

sources.name: Stjornarradid
sources.coverage: Ministry pages with policy documents, reports, committee work and the legislative programme for each session
sources.desc: The ministries' own site, and the place where the intention behind a regulation is usually explained if it is explained anywhere — the gazette publishes the regulation, not the reasoning.
sources.howto: Go to the responsible ministry and look for the case or the published report; the legislative programme (þingmálaskrá) for the session lists the bills the government intends to introduce and when.
sources.note: Policy material, not a source of law.

findLaw.task: Find the current text of an act
findLaw.steps: Open the act in the Lagasafn by number and year — 1944 number 33 for the Constitution — and read the consolidated text with its amendment notes. Then check the edition date on the collection and look in Stjórnartíðindi A for anything passed since.

Search Stjórnartíðindi for the item by number and year, remembering which division it belongs in: A for acts, B for regulations, tariffs and municipal by-laws, C for treaties. Publication here is what makes the rule binding, so the publication date is the date to record.

findLaw.task: Find the regulation under an act
findLaw.steps: Search the regulations collection by title, number or ministry, and check the authorising provision cited at the head of the regulation. Most Icelandic detail is at this level rather than in the act, and a regulation that exceeds its authorisation can be set aside.

Use the shared judgment search across the courts, or the Supreme Court's own 'Dómaleit'. Note the tier: since 2018 most appeals end at Landsréttur, and a Supreme Court judgment exists only where leave to appeal was granted, with the leave decisions published separately.

findLaw.task: Work out what a provision was meant to do
findLaw.steps: Find the bill in the Alþingi's session records and read the greinargerð published with it, then the committee opinions and the readings. For a regulation, look instead at the consultation portal, where the draft and the comments on it are published.

findLaw.task: Find the EEA rule behind an Icelandic one
findLaw.steps: Iceland is in the EEA, not the EU: an EU act applies only once taken into an annex of the EEA Agreement and implemented by an Icelandic act or regulation. Work from the implementing instrument, which cites the EEA decision, and use the EFTA Surveillance Authority's cases for how the obligation has been enforced.

Check the Government Offices' English legislation list, which carries the Constitution and a selection of acts in fields transacted internationally. If the act is not there, no official English version exists and the Icelandic text is the only one.
findLaw.source: Government of Iceland — legislation in English

subnational: Iceland is a unitary state with one tier below the centre: the sveitarfélög, municipalities, of which there are now around sixty after decades of amalgamation. They have no legislative power in the sense of enacting statutes; what they adopt are samþykktir and gjaldskrár — by-laws and tariffs on planning, waste, water, schools and local charges — under powers granted by act, and many of them require confirmation by the responsible minister before they take effect. The distinctive feature is publication: those by-laws and the municipalities' planning notices are published in the B division of Stjórnartíðindi, the national gazette, so Icelandic local law is centrally published and searchable rather than scattered across municipal websites. Disputes about whether a municipality has stayed within its powers go to the ordinary courts, and to the ministry exercising supervision over local government.
caveats: The Lagasafn is a periodic consolidation dated to a parliamentary session, not a continuously updated text, so the current wording is that edition plus anything published in Stjórnartíðindi since. The regulations collection is recent and publishes its own reservations about completeness; the authentic text of a regulation remains the item published in the B division. The two central sites, the Alþingi's and the gazette's older companion Lögbirtingablað, sit behind bot walls or are unreachable from outside Iceland, which affects automated access rather than browsers. Judgments are published with names in many cases, so a search can turn up more personal detail than in neighbouring countries. Iceland is not in the EU: an EU regulation has no force here of itself, and looking only at the EU instrument will tell you neither whether it applies nor from when. English translations are few, unofficial and often frozen at an old version. And a constitutional argument has no dedicated forum — there is no constitutional court, only the ordinary courts deciding the case in front of them.
